questions.question: For $f\colon U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ continuously differentiable near $a$, which condition on $Df(a)$ gives local injectivity near $a$?
options: $\operatorname{rank}Df(a)=m$ with $m\le n$
$Df(a)\neq0$, i.e. some entry is nonzero
$\operatorname{rank}Df(a)=n$ with $n\le m$
$\det Df(a)\neq0$, whatever $m$ and $n$ are

questions.question: Let $f\colon U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ be continuously differentiable on an open neighbourhood of $a\in U$. Which condition on $Df(a)$ guarantees local surjectivity near $a$?
options: $\operatorname{rank}Df(a)=m$ with $m\le n$
$\operatorname{rank}Df(a)=n$ with $n\le m$
Every entry of $Df(a)$ is nonzero
$\operatorname{rank}Df(a)\ge1$

questions.question: For $f(x,y)=(x+y^3,y)$, the Jacobian at $(0,0)$ is the identity matrix. How does the rank theorem apply at $(0,0)$?
options: Partial derivatives at $(0,0)$ exist, which alone supplies the required regularity.
The nonlinear term $y^3$ prevents the theorem from applying.
The Jacobian changes near $(0,0)$, which prevents the theorem from applying.
The components are polynomials, so $f$ is $C^1$; the Jacobian has full rank.

questions.question: Suppose a map from $\mathbb R^2$ to $\mathbb R^3$ has $Df(a)=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. What does its linearisation $h\mapsto Df(a)h$ do?
options: It reaches every vector in $\mathbb R^3$.
It sends only the zero input vector to zero.
It collapses a nonzero input direction because its third row is the sum of the first two.
It is invertible as a square matrix because its first two rows are independent.

questions.question: Let $f\colon\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ be $C^1$, with $Df(0,0)=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$. Which conclusion is guaranteed?
options: $f$ is locally bijective near $(0,0)$.
$f$ is bijective on all of $\mathbb R^2$.
$f$ is locally surjective but cannot be locally injective.
The theorem gives no conclusion because the determinant is negative.

questions.question: For $f(t)=(\cos t,\sin t,t)$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb R^3$, which local property does the rank theorem guarantee at every $t$?
options: Local surjectivity onto a neighbourhood in $\mathbb R^3$
No guaranteed local property
Local injectivity on an interval in $\mathbb R$
Local bijectivity onto a neighbourhood in $\mathbb R^3$

questions.question: For $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ from $\mathbb R^2$ to $\mathbb R$, at which points does the rank theorem guarantee local surjectivity?
options: Only at the origin, the minimiser
At every point of the plane
At no point, as $f\ge0$ everywhere
At every point except the origin

questions.question: For $f(x,y)=(x,y,xy)$ from $\mathbb R^2$ to $\mathbb R^3$, which local property near $(1,2)$ follows from the full-column-rank Jacobian criterion?
options: Local surjectivity onto $\mathbb R^3$
Local injectivity near $(1,2)$
Local bijectivity near $(1,2)$
Nothing, as the component $xy$ is not linear

questions.question: Define $f\colon\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ by $f(r,\theta)=(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)$, allowing all real $r$ and $\theta$. Where does the rank theorem guarantee local bijectivity?
options: At every point with $r\ne0$
Only at points with $\theta=0$
At every point, including $r=0$
Nowhere, because the map is periodic in $\theta$

questions.question: For $f(x,y)=(\sin x,y)$ at $a=(\pi/2,0)$, which conclusion is justified by the full-rank Jacobian criteria for local injectivity or surjectivity?
options: $f$ is locally bijective near $a$, as $f$ is $C^1$
$f$ is locally injective, as one column of $Df(a)$ is nonzero
$f$ is locally surjective, as $\operatorname{rank}Df(a)\ge1$
Nothing: $\det Df(a)=0$, so no part of it applies

questions.question: The maps $f(x)=x^3$ and $g(x)=x^2$ both have derivative zero at $0$. What does comparing their behaviour near $0$ establish?
options: A zero derivative prevents local injectivity for both maps.
The same singular linearisation can accompany different local behaviour.
Local surjectivity holds for both maps because both are continuous.
The rank theorem distinguishes the two maps using their derivatives at $0$.

questions.question: The map $f(x,y)=(\mathrm{e}^x\cos y,\mathrm{e}^x\sin y)$ has $\det Df=\mathrm{e}^{2x}\ne0$ everywhere. What follows?
options: $f$ is one-to-one on the whole plane $\mathbb R^2$.
$f$ maps onto every point of the plane $\mathbb R^2$.
$f$ is locally bijective near every point.
$f$ has a global inverse defined on all of $\mathbb R^2$.

questions.question: Why can a $C^1$ map $f\colon\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^2$ never satisfy the local-injectivity rank condition?
options: Its Jacobian has rank at most $2$, but the condition requires rank $3$.
A rectangular Jacobian cannot satisfy either rank condition.
The condition requires three independent rows in its Jacobian.
A nonzero kernel prevents the Jacobian from having full row rank.

questions.question: For $f(x,y,z)=(x+2y,yz)$ from $\mathbb R^3$ to $\mathbb R^2$, at which points does the full-row-rank Jacobian criterion guarantee local surjectivity?
options: Only at the points with $x\neq0$
Only at the origin
At every point of $\mathbb R^3$
Everywhere except where $y=z=0$

questions.question: For the linear map $f(x,y)=(x+y,\ 2x+2y)$, what can be said near any point $a$?
options: Locally bijective, as every linear map is
Locally injective, as no entry of $Df$ is zero
Neither locally injective nor surjective
Locally surjective, as the condition $m\le n$ holds

questions.question: Let $f(x,y)=x+y$, $a=(1,1)$ and $0<|\varepsilon|<0.01$. How many solutions of $f(x,y)=2+\varepsilon$ lie in the open ball of radius $0.1$ centred at $a$?
options: Infinitely many solutions, forming part of a line
Exactly one solution, as full row rank guarantees uniqueness
No solutions, as the target differs from $f(a)$
Exactly two solutions, one for each input coordinate

questions.question: Define $f\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ by $f(0)=0$ and $f(x)=x+2x^2\sin(1/x)$ for $x\ne0$. What can be said about applying the rank theorem at $0$?
options: It fails because the oscillation makes $f$ discontinuous at $0$.
Full rank holds at $0$, but the required continuous differentiability fails.
It fails because the oscillation prevents $f'(0)$ from existing.
It guarantees local injectivity because $f'(0)=1$ supplies every hypothesis.

questions.question: Let $f\colon\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ be $C^1$ and suppose $\operatorname{rank}Df(0,0)=1$. What must hold on a sufficiently small neighbourhood of $(0,0)$?
options: The rank is exactly $1$ throughout the neighbourhood.
The rank may be $0$ arbitrarily close to $(0,0)$.
The rank is $2$ at every other point in the neighbourhood.
The rank is at least $1$ throughout, but may rise to $2$.

questions.question: For $f(x,y)=(x^3+y,y)$, what can be said about a local inverse of $f$ near the output $(0,0)$?
options: No local inverse exists because $\det Df(0,0)=0$.
The local inverse exists and is differentiable at $(0,0)$.
It exists and is continuous, but not differentiable there
The local inverse is $g(u,v)=((u-v)^3,v)$, a polynomial map

questions.question: For $f(t)=(t^2-1,t^3-t)$, the rank theorem guarantees local injectivity at $t=1$. What is the largest radius $r>0$ for which $f$ is injective on the open interval $(1-r,1+r)$?
options: No positive radius works.
There is no finite upper bound.
